findings.title: Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive and unnormalized
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up `where(email: email)` with the exact string supplied, and neither BlockedEmail nor the validator normalizes case or surrounding whitespace before lookup/storage. A blocked address such as `bad@spam.com` can therefore be bypassed by registering as `Bad@Spam.com`, and administrators can also create duplicate block entries that differ only by case despite the unique index. Normalize (strip/downcase) the email both when saving BlockedEmail records and when checking should_block?.

findings.title: match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` reads the counter into memory and writes it back. Two concurrent registration attempts with the same blocked email will both read the same value and both write value+1, losing one increment and potentially overwriting last_match_at inconsistently. Use an atomic database increment (e.g. update_counters/increment_counter with a separate atomic last_match_at update) instead.

findings.title: Validation mutates BlockedEmail statistics and can count one attempt multiple times
findings.body: EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which saves match_count/last_match_at as a side effect of validation. Validation is not the same as a registration attempt: UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save` (which validates again), so a `do_nothing` match is counted twice for one signup, and any other code that merely checks validity (forms, console, related saves) inflates the statistics and performs a DB write during a nominally read-only check. Move the counter update out of the validator or make should_block? pure and record the match explicitly at the point of an actual blocked attempt.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array is shared mutable state on the controller prototype
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` defines one array on the prototype; `pushObject` in createAccount mutates that shared array rather than an instance-owned copy. Rejected addresses therefore persist across controller instances/recreation and can incorrectly mark an email invalid in a later, unrelated account-creation flow. Initialize rejectedEmails per instance (e.g. in init) instead of sharing the prototype array.
